questions.q: How can a trigger end up firing itself?
options: By declaring too many local variables
By using Trigger.isExecuting
By listing more than three trigger events
By performing DML on the same sObject the trigger is bound to, which is itself a new DML event on that object
questions.explain: A trigger's own update/insert/delete on its bound object is a DML event, and that event fires the trigger again — this is how recursion starts.

questions.q: What error does unchecked trigger recursion eventually produce?
options: System.LimitException: Too many SOQL queries
System.NullPointerException
System.Exception: Maximum trigger depth exceeded
DML.RequiredFieldMissing
questions.explain: If recursive re-firing isn't stopped, Salesforce eventually aborts the transaction with a maximum trigger depth exceeded error.

questions.q: Why does a static Boolean flag set to true during the first pass remain true when the trigger re-enters via its own update call?
options: It doesn't — each trigger invocation gets a fresh copy of every static variable
Static variables persist for the duration of the whole transaction, not just one method call, so the flag set earlier is still visible on re-entry
Boolean values are always true by default in Apex
The flag is stored in the database between invocations
questions.explain: Static variables live for the life of one transaction; a flag set at the start of the first trigger run is still set when that same transaction's recursive call re-enters the handler.

questions.q: What is the main downside of using a single shared static Boolean as a recursion guard, compared with tracking specific record Ids?
options: Booleans are slower to evaluate than Sets
A plain boolean can't be declared as static at all
It blocks all re-entry while set, which can skip genuinely new, unrelated records processed later in the same transaction
Boolean guards only work on the Account object
questions.explain: A single shared flag is all-or-nothing — it can't distinguish 'this exact record was already handled' from 'something is already running', so it risks skipping unrelated records that should still be processed.

questions.q: In the static Set<Id> guard pattern, what determines whether a record is reprocessed?
options: Whether its Id is already present in the static Set tracked by the handler
Whether Trigger.isBefore is true
Whether the record was the first one in Trigger.new
Whether more than 200 records are in the batch
questions.explain: Checking processedAccountIds.contains(acc.Id) guards per specific record rather than blocking the whole handler, so unrelated records aren't skipped.
